inferences.claim: This type is a chain of four fixed filter sections and an output gain: a low shelf, two peaking sections that share one law, a high shelf. The low shelf is one pole and one zero. Each parameter byte selects from a short table rather than driving a formula -- a gain answers over twenty-five values and sticks at both ends, a corner has two states, a width has five entries and returns the first for anything past them, a centre moves in equal steps of log frequency for every eighth value of its byte.

inferences.why: the comparison was made and carries no verdict yet
inferences.claim: This type is eight first-order all-pass sections in series, summed with the dry signal rather than averaged with it, running at thirty-two kilohertz. One byte moves every section's corner together, which puts four cancellations in the audible band at fixed ratios read in the tangent of frequency -- so they crowd towards each other in hertz as the byte takes them up, and the top ones leave the band rather than staying four.
inferences.named: a phaser as the period built one: an all-pass ladder mixed back with the input

inferences.claim: The byte beside this type's manual is the gain of a feedback loop closed around the all-pass cascade, and it is not a second mix and not a resonance inside the sections. A cascade passes everything at unit gain, so summing it with the dry signal reaches six decibels where the two arrive in phase and no further; the profile reaches 18.87 dB, which a sum would need nearly eight helpings of the cascade to do. What the loop puts there instead is a resonance between each pair of notches -- where the cascade comes back in phase with itself and the return adds up -- while the notches stay where the closed reading put them. Two further things about it are readable, one at each end of the band. The return arrives one sample late, which is what a part computing a sample at a time has no choice about, and the phase that costs is nothing at the bottom and half a circle at half the rate: at the top of the band it turns the highest resonance into the cancellation it would otherwise have been, which the unit does and an instantaneous loop does not. And the return will not carry the bottom of the band: the lowest resonance is largest at 105 Hz and has fallen thirteen decibels by 25, by more the harder the loop is driven and by nothing at all when the loop is open -- which puts one pole of a high pass inside the loop and nowhere else in the chain. The loop gains themselves are a readout of seventeen settings and no law is claimed on them. What the seventeen do settle is that there is something to claim: the gain moves at every one of them, and the two that share the top four bits of the byte come back 0.0675 apart -- further than any neighbouring pair of the sweep -- so this byte is not the sixteen-entry table the byte one address along on the same type turned out to be.
inferences.named: a feedback path around an all-pass cascade, a sample late and blocked at DC

inferences.claim: A rotary's slow rate byte indexes the same printed table every other rate byte on this unit indexes -- the wide one, picked by the `0.05 - 10.0` the page prints against it, with no constant of its own anywhere in it. What the rotary adds is that the entry is where a rotor is sent and not where it ends up. Sent down, it arrives exactly -- which is measured and not inferred: the same byte written after a faster one, with no reset between, comes back on its entry where the same byte written after a reset comes back short of it. Sent up, it stops a fixed distance short: 0.245 Hz on the low rotor and 0.062 on the high, holding to a thousandth of a hertz from the corner to the top of the byte and across both places the table's own step changes. And where the distance to the entry is narrower than that, the rotor barely sets off, so five entries of the low rotor's table return one rate and the high rotor moves a fifth of an entry across the one entry of its own. The width of that flat stretch and the size of the gap are the same number, which is what separates this from a constant subtracted after a lookup: read the gap off the top of the sweep alone and it places the corner, which neither half of the fit was shown. The distance is set by the acceleration byte the page prints against each rotor, and the two rotors are one routine reached twice: at every one of nine settings of that byte the two gaps agree to a median of 2.8 per cent, so the four to one between them is the two defaults and not the two rotors. What that byte does is a claim of its own beside this one.
inferences.named: a first-order lag done with an arithmetic right shift, which underflows climbing and floors falling

inferences.claim: A rotary's acceleration byte is read through its top four bits, and the sixteen entries that leaves are what the rotor's loop multiplies the difference by before shifting it. So the distance the rotor stops short of the rate entry it was aimed at is one constant divided by what the entry holds. What the entries hold is a sequence: the first ten count up, one through ten, and then they double -- twelve, sixteen, thirty-two, sixty-four, a hundred and twenty-eight. 14 of the sixteen are readable and 12 of those land on that sequence inside what their own take told a rate apart to, with one constant over the whole table and nothing else fitted. The last one does not: it reads 168 where the doubling says 256, five times what the take resolves, and it is published as the number it is. The byte is not a shift count, which is what a four-bit acceleration invited: the distance does not halve per step of it, and the near-four between the two rotors' defaults is where those two defaults happen to sit in this table. The two rotors are one routine reached twice -- at nine settings of the byte their distances agree to a median of 2.8 per cent. And the constant, 0.9768 Hz, names the clock a fifth time by a route none of the other four used: it is a rate divided by a power of two, and at thirty-two kilohertz that power is 14.9996 while at forty-four and forty-eight no integer power comes within four tenths.
inferences.named: a four-bit acceleration that multiplies the difference before the shift

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim: The filter a stereo flanger puts in front of itself and the filter a stereo chorus puts in front of itself are one section. Swept at every setting the chorus's was published at -- 15 of them across the two filter shapes the byte beside it offers -- the two types return the same skirt over a hundred and thirteen twelfth-octave bands to a median of 0.08 dB at worst, where those runs repeat themselves to 0.08 dB and where one step of the byte being swept moves the profile by at least 0.15 dB. The agreement is at the floor and the thing it is being told from is two to ten times the floor, so this is the reading saying the same section twice and not the reading running out. The page prints the two types' parameter lists identically -- same order, same addresses, same ranges -- with one entry in the flanger's that the chorus has not got, a feedback level in the slot the chorus leaves empty. That list is what made the question worth asking and it is not what answers it; what this file claims is the front end, and what the loop is around is queued.

A filter byte's corner sits on a single pole, and both filters this type's type byte selects are one pole each. The low pass falls six decibels an octave through the middle of the band and the high pass the same the other way; neither is a biquad and neither is two poles cascaded, which would be twelve. The low pass carries the zero the bilinear transform leaves at half the rate, and that is what makes a clock readable off it: the skirt bends from 5.7 decibels an octave between 800 Hz and 1.6 kHz to 10.3 between 6.4 and 12.7 kHz, which puts half the rate just above the top of the band and the rate at thirty-two kilohertz. Read at forty-four or forty-eight it is four times worse and leans. The high pass names the order and cannot name the rate: its corners are all under 500 Hz, its zero is at nothing, and the place a warp would show is its own flat passband. One corner table serves both -- at the four settings both were read the two agree to within 0.064 octaves, which is what this reading resolves.
inferences.named: a one-pole section, the same one written twice with its numerator changed

inferences.claim: A delay's damping byte is one pole inside the delay's own feedback loop, and it is the pole written the cheapest way there is: a running average, one multiply and one state, with no zero at half the rate. Inside rather than once on the way out, which is read off how a held note builds: with the byte at the position the page prints as the filter out the build is 18.3 dB and it is the same in every band, and with the filter in it falls away above a frequency that moves more than four octaves across the byte. A filter outside the loop is the same shape in both windows and cancels between them. That is not the section the same part's chorus filter byte sits on. A pole put through the bilinear transform keeps a zero at half the rate and its skirt bends steeper as it climbs towards it; this one has no zero, so its skirt stops cutting and levels off -- and the profile does level off, on every one of the ten settings the run asked, at a different depth each time. Where a profile levels off names the pole outright with nothing fitted, because the depth is one minus the coefficient over one plus it. Scored through the same takes the cheap pole is sixteen times the bilinear one's median and is the only candidate of eight whose residual does not lean. And it names the clock a fourth time, by a route none of the first three used: the coefficient that puts the corner where the page prints it depends on the rate, so a corner fitted freely from each setting's own skirt lands on the printed third octaves to a five-hundredth of an octave at thirty-two kilohertz and a twentieth at forty-four -- high at every setting, which is a lean and not a scatter.
inferences.named: a one-multiply pole, the running average a fixed-point part damps a delay's repeats with

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim: The byte a page prints `Small/BltIn/2-Stk/3-Stk` against is one table of four fixed responses, written once and reached from more than one place, and it sits after the drive stage rather than shaping what goes into it. One table, because an entry read on a type that is nothing but a drive stage and the same entry read from inside a pair land a median 0.18 dB apart across a hundred and thirteen twelfth-octave bands, where the same reading puts two different entries of the table 1.96 dB apart or more -- so the reading separates the entries by better than an order of magnitude over what it says separates these. After the drive stage, because the pair was read once with each of the two drive characters its selector offers, and those characters put out measurably different spectra: a median 3.87 dB apart in shape and 9.99 dB at their widest, one carrying nine decibels more above eight kilohertz and the other seven more through the midrange. A filter shaping the input to a nonlinearity does not divide out of the result, because the nonlinearity remaps whatever spectrum it is given; a filter after one does, exactly. The ratio between two amp entries is 0.09 dB apart between the two characters, which is under the runs' own repeats -- so it divides out, and the filter is on the output. The switch beside the byte is what puts the table in the path at all: at Off the profile is its own reference to a median of a seventh of a decibel, and at On it is a bandpass, 10.7 dB down through the bottom octave and 3.2 down above eight kilohertz against 4.9 up through the two to four kilohertz octave.
inferences.named: a fixed cabinet response, one short filter per entry, multiplying the drive stage's output

inferences.why: the comparison was made and carries no verdict yet
inferences.claim: An azimuth byte does not scale an angle and does not have 128 values. Two is added to it, the result is shifted right two places, the centre is taken off, and what is left is stopped at 15 either way -- so the byte reaches 31 positions 12 degrees apart, from L180 through 0 to R180. The added two is the rounding of a divide by four and nothing else: without it every position would sit a byte off the one the page prints. Twenty nine of the positions are 4 byte values wide and the two poles are 6, which is not a widening of those positions but the clamp taking the two values at each end of the byte the shift would have carried past them. The two poles are one place: half a turn to the left is half a turn to the right, and the page writes that into both cells rather than leaving it to be noticed.

inferences.why: the comparison was made and carries no verdict yet
inferences.claim: A byte printed `D> 0E - D 0<E` is two multipliers, each of them the byte's distance from a corner divided by fifty, truncated onto a grid of a hundred and twenty-eight and clamped at both ends -- and the two are offset so that they meet at full rather than crossing. The half that goes past the effect holds at its dry-end level for every setting up to and including 64, leaves it at 65, and is at nothing from 114 on. Read every count over both corners, thirty-two settings land within a sixth of a step of `min(1, floor((114 - n) * 128 / 50) / 128)` on the ramp and within half a step anywhere, and each of the three numbers in it is pinned by the reading: a quarter of a count on the width costs six times the residual, rounding instead of truncating costs seven times it, and the multipliers sit a twelfth of a step from the grid's entries where a number on no grid would sit a quarter of one away. Read in the window the return arrives in, the effect's own half rises for the last time at 64 and holds from 65, ten times what the takes repeat either way, so it is the direct half reflected through 128 rather than through 127: `min(1, floor((n - 14) * 128 / 50) / 128)`, whose corner and the direct half's sum to 128, and which meets the direct half at full at exactly 64. That half is read on two of the three types and carried by a shape rather than a threshold: truncation makes the four steps over the corner uneven, and reflected through 128 they are predicted at 0.220, 0.144, 0.211 and 0.206 of a decibel and read within 0.010 of that on one type and 0.031 on the other, where reflecting through 127 is out by 0.200 and 0.175. So the middle of the byte carries both halves at once and stands three decibels over either end, which is the opposite sign to a crossfade and not flat. Both ends reach true nothing: the direct window at the effect end falls to 1.1 decibels over the same take's own lead, which is the interface and not the unit. The law was found on one type at one count and holds on the two others, read at eight counts on a different day, to seven tenths of a step.
inferences.named: min(1, floor((114 - n) * 128 / 50) / 128) past the effect and min(1, floor((n - 14) * 128 / 50) / 128) through it, which is the same law reflected through 128 rather than through 127, so the two meet at full at 64

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim: Every effect parameter this unit powers up holding is a value its own manual prints as that parameter's default. 575 parameters across sixty-five types were in a position to disagree and none did, 154 of them at a byte the printing leaves no choice about.

A frequency byte does not drive a formula and does not have a hundred and twenty-eight values. Its top four bits index a table of sixteen entries, so eight settings share each entry, and the entries are the named third octaves between the two frequencies the page prints against that address -- with one that is not. On 200 - 6.3k, fifteen of the sixteen sit within 0.07 octaves of 200, 250, 400, 500, 630, 800, 1k, 1.25k, 1.6k, 2k, 2.5k, 3.15k, 4k, 5k and 6.3k, a median 0.03 and under what a twelfth-octave reading resolves. The third entry sits at 279 Hz where the series says 315, which is 0.18 octaves and two bands, and it is the only entry the reading and the series disagree about. Both mid sections return that same 279, and they return the whole of the first four entries to within 0.002 octaves of each other, so the two index one table rather than two. Read across its own eight settings the entry does not move -- 279.1, 278.7, 278.8 and 279.0 at 16, 17, 20 and 23 -- and the settings either side of it return the entries either side, so the stride is eight and the number in the table is 279.
inferences.named: a third-octave coefficient table indexed by the byte's high nibble, with one entry that is not a third octave

inferences.claim: A gain byte printed -12 - +12 is decibels, one per step, offset by sixty-four. It answers over a window of twenty-five values from 52 to 76 and returns the nearest end for everything outside. And the two of them that forty-three types carry with no frequency printed beside either are this unit's equaliser's own shelf pair with the frequency byte taken away and pinned to its first printed entry.

An insertion effect's output level byte is a multiplier stored as a whole number over a hundred and twenty-seven, and that multiplier is not the byte. Every one of the hundred and twenty-five settings the run could read returns a gain that sits on the 1/127 grid: a median 0.0225 of a step away, against 0.2185 for the next best denominator of the sixty-one asked and 0.25 for a number that sat on no grid at all. What the entries are is a curve and not a formula -- the multiplier is three quarters of the byte over the bottom quarter of the range and rises to the byte itself at the top, and no law in the catalogue crosses that. The byte read straight as the multiplier is out by a median 1.61 decibels and by 3.53 at setting 9.
inferences.named: a stored table of seven-bit multipliers, one per setting

inferences.claim: A byte printed `L63 - 0 - R63` is one multiplier a side, the same pair on types whose front halves have nothing in common, and what stops it twenty-five decibels short of silence is not the multiplier. Read one band at a time the two channels separate by 33.7 decibels more in some bands than in others at the ends of the sweep and alike in all of them through the middle, against the same pair of channels with the effect taken out of the path separating alike everywhere to 0.1 of a decibel. A pair of multipliers has no frequency in it and cannot do that. Allow one term added after the pan and nineteen settings of twenty bands come back as one multiplier each, over 342 readings to a median of 0.17 decibels -- agreeing with the broadband balance to a tenth through the middle of the sweep and departing from it by two decibels at the last byte, which is where the broadband reading was reading the added term. The table's two sides are one table read in opposite directions, 0.54 of a decibel apart at worst over 17 settings, and its centre entry sits 2.44 decibels under its end -- neither the 3.01 of a constant-power pair nor the 6.02 of a straight crossfade.

A rate byte does not drive a formula. It indexes a printed table of whole steps of a twentieth of a hertz, and there are two such tables, told apart by the range the page prints against the address. The narrow one is 128 entries of 0.05 Hz, from 0.05 to 6.40. The wide one shares those entries as far as 5.00 Hz at setting 99, then steps by 0.10 to 7.00 at 119 and by 0.50 to 10.00 at 125 -- 126 entries, so the last two settings of the byte have no entry of their own and return the last one. One table serves every type: the same twenty-one slots across nineteen effect types answer to it with no per-type constant anywhere.

A delay-time byte does not scale a time and does not run a formula. It indexes a ladder of round decimal milliseconds whose step changes a few times over the byte, and every entry is then cut back to a whole step of a clock running at 32000 Hz -- which is what a delay addressed as a sample count does to a time written in milliseconds. Which ladder a slot is on is picked by the conversion column the effect list cites beside it, not by the range the page prints -- two slots print the same range and cite different columns, and they return ladders fifty milliseconds apart. On 0 - 500m the step is a tenth of a millisecond to setting fifty, then a half to sixty, then one to ninety, then ten to a hundred and sixteen, then twenty to a hundred and twenty-six; on 0 - 100m it is the same tenth to fifty and half to sixty, then one to a hundred, then two to a hundred and twenty-five; on 200m - 990m/1sec the byte starts at two hundred milliseconds and steps five to setting seventy, then ten to a hundred and fifteen, where it reaches one second; on 0m - 635m the step never changes at all -- five milliseconds from the first setting to the last; and 0m - 500m, which the page spells with an m the other five-hundred range does not have, is that range's ladder entry for entry. Four of the five reach the printed end before the byte ends and repeat it at every setting above, and the fifth reaches it at its last setting, so where a ladder stops is read off the record in both directions. The cut is not a detail of the ladder: it is what the settings at the short end actually return, and it is what decides which settings the reading brings back a tall peak for. It is also why two of the five ranges say nothing about the clock -- every entry on them is five milliseconds or more, which is already a whole step of it, so there is no setting at which the two readings differ. One slot of the five does not read its ladder from wherever it is asked. On the type whose delay glides, a setting reached from below is short of its cited column by a thousand and sixteen whole samples of the same clock, and the same setting reached from above returns that column times a hundred and twenty-seven over a hundred and twenty-eight exactly -- the same one-byte ratio every entry here carries. So the shortfall the sweep found is the sweep's own direction and not a second regime in the table, and the byte the page prints beside it as an acceleration is worth exactly half of it, from its top bit alone and from no other bit in the nibble.

The tone controls these two types carry are one pair of first-order shelves whose corners are fixed and have no byte: a low shelf at 161 Hz and a high shelf at or above 5187 Hz. The pair is the same pair on both types -- fitted to each type on its own the low corners land 0.0 octaves apart and the high ones 0.0119, and one shared pair scores each record as well as its own fit does. The section is one pole and one zero: a unit-slope second-order shelf is two to three times worse on the median of every one of the four records and three times worse at its worst, and its worst band is in the shelf's own transition every time. The gain is not fitted here at all -- it is the window the gain class closed on, twenty-five values centred on 64 that stick at both ends, and the same window that type 01 00 was read with.
inferences.named: a fixed first-order shelf pair, the part's tone control

inferences.why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
inferences.claim: A modulation wave byte indexes five fixed shapes and computes nothing, and four of the five are the shapes the page names them. Read on two types that drive different quantities with the same byte -- one swinging its output's level by more than the whole of its own mean, the other swinging the balance between its channels by forty decibels -- the entry printed `Tri` returns a triangle, `Sqr` a square and `Saw1` and `Saw2` a sawtooth, each nearer the shape it is named after than any other by both of the two readings taken, on both types, 8 readings out of 8. `Saw1` and `Saw2` are one shape run two ways: no reading of magnitudes can separate them, which the two candidates sitting exactly zero apart under both scores says outright, and what separates them is that one spends nine tenths of its cycle climbing and the other one tenth. The fifth entry is not what it is printed. `Sin` carries a third harmonic of four to six hundredths where a sine has none and a triangle has a ninth, and a fifth harmonic of two thousandths where a triangle has a twenty-fifth -- so it is neither, and it is a sine made cheaply. Which cheap sine is not settled and is queued. The shape is a shape of a multiplier and not of a level: the same cycles come back clean read in amplitude and warped read in decibels, which is what a gain swung linearly does to a logarithm and not what a gain swung in decibels would do to either.
inferences.named: a table of five fixed modulator shapes, indexed by a byte, multiplying
